title: Two knights against a pawn
summary: Two knights alone cannot force mate, but against a pawn they can: the Troitsky line, the blockade, the moment to let the pawn go and Black's defence.
part.pawnHelps.title: The pawn that helps
part.pawnHelps.summary: Why one extra pawn for Black makes the mate possible, and why one is enough.
part.zugzwang.title: Troitsky's position
part.zugzwang.summary: A mutual zugzwang: whoever has to move loses. And with the king caught, even a pawn past the line loses.
part.line.title: The Troitsky line
part.line.summary: Where to blockade the pawn, and why the blockader is a knight.
part.drive.title: King to the corner
part.drive.summary: One knight holds the pawn; the king and the other knight drive the black king to the corner.
part.release.title: Releasing the pawn
part.release.summary: When to let the pawn go: the mate must come before it promotes. Seitz, Nice, 1931.
part.summary.title: Summary
part.summary.summary: Four rules for your games, the fifty moves and the whole mate in the practical challenge.
step.t_help: King on f7, knights on f5 and d2, and the black king stuck on h7. The d2 knight is holding the pawn on d3. White wants to mate: how?
step.t_help.hint1: Imagine the same position without the black pawn. What happens when the black king runs out of squares and nobody is giving check?
step.t_help.hint2: The d2 knight has a better job than watching the pawn. Let the pawn go: every move it makes is a move the black king does not have to make.
step.d_help: Watch the black pawn working for White.
step.d_help.m1: 1.Ne4. The d2 knight lets go of the pawn and heads for f6. This and 1.Nf3 are the only winning moves.
step.d_help.m2: 1...d2. The pawn runs to promote. After 1...Kh8 Black would lose just the same.
step.d_help.m3: 2.Nf6+. The black king only has h8.
step.d_help.m4: 2...Kh8, the only move: g8, g7 and g6 belong to the white king, and h6 to the f5 knight.
step.d_help.m5: 3.Ne7! Now the black king has no square at all. Without the pawn, this would be stalemate.
step.d_help.m6: 3...d1=Q. The black king has no square, so Black has to move the pawn, and the new queen arrives too late.
step.d_help.m7: 4.Ng6, mate. The pawn gave Black the one move they needed not to be stalemated.
step.t_zz: In the last three chapters the pawn was on the line. Here it has already crossed it: the line square on the d-file is d4, and the pawn is on d3. White to move and win, and only one move works. Which one, and why?
step.t_zz.hint1: Think about who has the move after yours. A knight that leaves a square and comes back to it always spends an even number of moves.
step.t_zz.hint2: Compare it with the position at the start of the lesson, with the white king on f7 and the black king on h7. Which black move takes the black king back there?
step.zzWhy: 1.Kf7! And we reach Troitsky's most famous position, with Black to move. Black's only move is 1...Kh7, and we are back at the position from the start of the lesson: 2.Ne4 d2 3.Nf6+ Kh8 4.Ne7 d1=Q 5.Ng6, mate. But if, in Troitsky's position, it were White to move, it would be a draw: White cannot pass the move. It is a mutual zugzwang: whoever has the move is worse off. And notice: with the black king caught, the pawn past the line does not save Black. When the king is already in the net, let the pawn move and stop it again.
step.d_zzDraw: Now Troitsky's position with White to move, and you are Black. This is the defence Averbakh and Chekhover gave: White tries everything with the king.
step.d_zzDraw.m1: 1.Kf6. The white king tries another way.
step.d_zzDraw.m3: 2.Kf7, back again. White is trying to lose a tempo with the king.
step.d_zzDraw.m4: 2...Kh8, the only move: g8, g7 and g6 belong to the white king, and h6 to the knight.
step.d_zzDraw.m5: 3.Kg6. Now the white king watches h7 and g7.
step.d_zzDraw.m6: 3...Kg8, the only move: h7 and g7 belong to the white king.
step.d_zzDraw.m7: 4.Ng7. The knight watches e8 and h5.
step.d_zzDraw.m8: 4...Kf8, the only move that holds. After 4...Kh8? White would win: the black king would be stuck in the corner, with White to move.
step.d_zzDraw.m9: 5.Kf6, closing the black king in from the front.
step.d_zzDraw.m10: 5...Kg8, the only move: e7, f7 and e8 are taken.
step.d_zzDraw.m12: 6...Kh7! The only move. After 6...Kh8?, White would play 7.Kg6 and Black, to move, would lose. With the king on h7, White cannot repeat the trick, and it is a draw.
step.zzMove: Now the other line: after 6...Kh8?, instead of 6...Kh7, it is your move. Put Black in zugzwang and finish the job.
step.zzMove.hint: 7.Kg6 first: the black king will only have g8. Then 8.Ne4: the d2 knight lets the pawn go.
step.zzMove.done: That's it. 7.Kg6 and 8.Ne4 were the only winning moves. The rest is the pattern you already know: the pawn moves, and the knights deliver mate.
step.reBlock: The black king is already caught on h7, and the pawn on d4 is about to cross the line.
step.reBlock.hint: Don't chase the pawn: wait for it. Which square in front of it can the b1 knight reach in one move?
step.reBlock.done: 1.Nd2! The knight waits for the pawn: after 1...d3 it is held again, past the line, and we are back at the position from the start of the lesson. With the black king in the net, a pawn past the line does not save Black.
step.t_line: In the previous chapter the pawn was already held by a knight. Here it is still free. The black king is in the corner, but there is no net yet. What is White's first job?
step.t_line.hint1: Forget the black king for a moment. Look only at the pawn.
step.t_line.hint2: If the pawn reaches g5, g4 and beyond, can you still hold it and mate in time? Where does it have to be stopped?
step.lineWhy: 1.Ng5! was the only winning move. The knight stops the pawn on g6, and g6 is one of the squares of the Troitsky line: a4, b6, c5, d4, e4, f5, g6 and h4. His rule: if a knight blockades the pawn on this line, or behind it, White wins wherever the kings are. The reason is time. While the pawn is stuck, White drives the black king calmly; when the pawn is released, it still needs several moves to promote, and the mate comes first. Notice the line is not straight: on the b- and g-files it sits further back, on b6 and g6. With the colours reversed, the line turns upside down: a5, b3, c4, d5, e5, f4, g3 and h5.
step.lineMove: The pawn on f5 is on the line, but nobody is blockading it. Stop it now, before it gets past.
step.lineMove.hint: The square in front of the pawn is f4. Which knight gets there, and with what bonus?
step.lineMove.done: 1.Nf4+! The knight blockades the pawn on the line and gives check as well. It was the only winning move: without it, the pawn would cross the line with 1...f4.
step.t_drive: The pawn is already held on the line: what about the black king? The g5 knight blockades the pawn on g6, and the black king is on g8. What is the plan? Who works and who stays put?
step.t_drive.hint1: The g5 knight does not need to leave yet. Which squares near the black king is it already watching?
step.t_drive.hint2: The white king and the e4 knight do the pushing. The black king's destination is the h8 corner.
step.driveWhy: 1.Kf6 is the first step. The g5 knight does two jobs at once: it holds the pawn and watches f7 and h7, two important squares near the corner. That is why it stays put. The white king and the other knight drive the black king to h8. Only at the end, with the black king caught, does the g5 knight leave.
step.d_drive: Watch the king and the free knight working together. The g5 knight does not move.
step.d_drive.m1: 1.Kf6. The white king takes e7, f7 and g7.
step.d_drive.m2: 1...Kf8. The black king looks for a way out through the centre.
step.d_drive.m3: 2.Nd6. The knight takes e8 and f7: the black king only has g8.
step.d_drive.m4: 2...Kg8, back again: e8 and f7 belong to the knight, e7 and g7 to the white king.
step.d_drive.m5: 3.Ke7. The white king takes f8 and f7.
step.d_drive.m6: 3...Kg7. The black king uses the square the white king left.
step.d_drive.m7: 4.Ndf7. Now h8 and h6 are covered, and the black king only has g8.
step.d_drive.m8: 4...Kg8, the only move: the black king can no longer leave the corner.
step.d_drive.m9: 5.Ne5. The knight goes round to reach g4.
step.d_drive.m10: 5...Kh8. The black king is already in the corner.
step.d_drive.m11: 6.Ng4. From here the knight watches f6 and h6. The black king is left with a tiny corner: g7, g8 and h8.
step.d_drive.m12: 6...Kg7. The net is ready. In the next chapter, the moment to let the pawn go.
step.driveMove: Now you. It is the same position mirrored: the b5 knight holds the pawn on b6, and the black king is on b8. Drive it to the corner with the king and the d4 knight.
step.driveMove.hint: First 1.Kc6. Then 2.Ne6, taking c7 and d8.
step.driveMove.done: Well done. The b5 knight never moved: it held the pawn and watched a7 and c7 while the king and the other knight did the pushing.
step.t_release: The black king is in the corner: time to let go? The black king is caught between g7, g8 and h8, and the g5 knight is still holding the pawn. Find the winning sequence.
step.t_release.hint1: Count the moves the pawn needs to reach g1 once it is free.
step.t_release.hint2: The g5 knight can leave with check. Where does the black king go after that?
step.releaseWhy: Now is the time: 1.Ne6+. The g5 knight leaves with check and releases the pawn. The pawn needs five moves to reach g1. White needs about as many, but the first is check and the black king spends moves running: the mate arrives first. And the pawn's moves are exactly what prevents stalemate: while the black king has no squares, Black moves the pawn. The rule: release the blockade when the black king is already in the net and the mate comes before the promotion.
step.releaseMove: Back to our position. Now it is you: release the pawn with check and mate before it promotes.
step.releaseMove.done: The pawn is free, and the mate comes before the promotion. Releasing the blockade at the right moment is half of this ending.
step.fifty: And there is the fifty-move rule. Here the pawn is on e4, on the line, still free, and only 1.Ne3, which blockades it, keeps the win. But White wins only without the rule: the first pawn move or capture would come after some sixty-seven moves, and the rule ends the game before that. The longest mate in this ending takes more than a hundred moves. In practice it helps a lot to have the pawn stuck well behind the line, or the black king already near the corner.
step.rules: Four rules for your games. One: blockade the pawn with a knight on the Troitsky line, or behind it; the king is no good as a blockader, and the last pawn is never taken. Two: the blockading knight stays put; the king and the other knight drive the black king to the corner. Three: release the blockade only when the mate comes before the promotion; with the black king caught, even a pawn past the line loses, and the king can pass the move with a triangle. Four, with Black: with the pawn past the line, take the king into the drawing zone, away from the mating corner.
step.playIntro: Now the whole mate. The pawn on g6 is on the line but not yet blockaded. Lock it up, take the black king to the corner, release the pawn at the right moment and mate.
ex.e07: The pawn on a3 is free and racing to a1. Is there time to mate? Find the winning move.
ex.e07.hint: Do not give check. A king move leaves the black king with no squares.
ex.e07.solution: 1.Kf7! It was the only winning move. The black king has no squares and only the pawn can move: 1...a2. Then 2.Ne5 (2.Nf6 also works), and after 2...a1=Q, 3.Neg6 is mate. The pawn is fast, but the mate is faster.
ex.e09: The black king is caught on h6, but the pawn can still run. Find the three moves that keep the win.
ex.e09.hint: First take the black king's squares, so that Black has to move the pawn. Then stop the pawn again, even past the line.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Ndf6! The black king has no squares: h5 and h7 belong to the f6 knight, g5 to the e4 knight, g7 to the white king. Black has to play 1...g5. The pawn has crossed the line, but the black king is already caught: 2.Ng3! waits for the pawn (2.Nxg5? captures the last pawn and draws), and after 2...g4 it is blockaded again. Finally 3.Nfe4!, the only winning move: the knight watches g5, the square the black king would escape through, and the blockaded pawn cannot move, so the black king has to head for the corner with 3...Kh7. Then 4.Nf5 Kh8 5.Ng5 g3 6.Nh4 g2 7.Ng6, mate. 1.Kf6? also keeps the win, but lets the black king run out via h5 and g4, and the hunt starts again from scratch.
key.help: Two knights alone can't mate, but here the black pawn helps: since Black can still move it, there's no stalemate, and the mate comes.
key.troitsky: A two-way zugzwang: if White is to move, it's a draw; if Black is to move, Black loses.
key.line: The black pawn is held by a knight on a square of the Troitsky line. If the blockade happens no further than this line, White wins.
key.horwitzKling: The knight that was holding the pawn lets it go at the right moment: the pawn's moves avoid stalemate while the other white pieces build the mate.
key.karpov: Topalov against Karpov, Monte Carlo, 2000, a rapid game: Karpov let the draw slip, and here, with Black to move, there is no defence left.
history: Two knights and a king cannot force mate against a lone king: at the last moment there is always a stalemate. The odd thing is that if the opponent still has a pawn, mate can become possible again: the pawn gives Black moves to make, and the stalemate disappears. It's an ending full of surprises that baffles even strong players. The man who unravelled it was the Russian Alexey Troitsky, one of the greatest study composers in history, who worked on it for decades and published his analysis in 1937; years later it turned out to be astonishingly accurate. Troitsky starved to death in 1942, during the siege of Leningrad. The first master win with this ending came in 1931, in Nice, when Adolf Seitz beat Eugene Znosko-Borovsky. Even Anatoly Karpov stumbled here: in 2000, in a rapid game in Monte Carlo, he lost a drawn position to Veselin Topalov.
practice: Now the real ending: the pawn still on g7, free, and the black king on g8. Lock the pawn up, take the king to the corner and release the blockade at the right moment.
ex.e12: Topalov–Karpov, Monte Carlo 2000. The pawn on g4 is already past the line, but the g3 knight holds it. With the pawn past the line, the mate only works in some corners. Where does the black king go? Hold the draw.
ex.e12.hint: The white king and the d4 knight are already on the a1 side: that is where the mate arrives before the pawn promotes. Which way should your king go?
ex.e12.solution: 65...Kd2! (65...Kd1 also holds). The black king goes to the pawn's side, away from the a1 corner, and White cannot push it into a corner where the mate comes in time. 65...Kb1, 65...Kc1 and 65...Kb2, Karpov's move, lose: the black king heads for the a1 corner, where the white king and the knights build the net. In the game, Topalov gave the draw back with 67.Ndf5?, but Karpov went back toward the corner with 67...Kb2? (only 67...Kb1 held) and lost: on 74.Ne2 the g3 knight let the pawn go, because the mate was already coming before promotion.
ex.e11: Wang Yue–Anand, Nice 2009, a blindfold game. Now Black has the knights, and the white pawn on c3 is about to move. How do you stop it in a way that wins? Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: To win, the pawn must be held by a knight, on the Troitsky line or behind it. For a white pawn on the c-file, the line runs through c4.
ex.e11.solution: 61...Ne4! The knight heads for c5: after 62.c4, 62...Nc5! locks the pawn on the line, and from there Black wins. 61...Nd2 also wins. Anand played 61...Kc5 and blockaded the pawn with the king, the wrong piece: the win slipped away and the game was drawn. 61...Ne5 would only win without the fifty-move rule.
ex.e14: Study by Horwitz and Kling, 1851. Black has two pawns, the h2 pawn is one step from promoting and the black king attacks the f3 knight. Find the way out.
ex.e14.hint: Remember why the pawn helps: it prevents stalemate. One pawn is enough for that. Then the white king traps the black king in the corner.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Nxh2!! Kxh2. This time taking is right: the h3 pawn stays on the board, and it is enough to prevent stalemate. 2.Kf1! Kh1 3.Kf2 Kh2 4.Ne3 Kh1 5.Nf1 h2 and 6.Ng3 is mate: the pawn on h2 blocks its own king's escape. The full study starts three moves earlier, with two knight checks and the white king heading to e1.
ex.e13: Study by Chéron, 1955. The pawn on g3 is already past the line, but the g2 knight holds it and the black king is caught in the corner. If it were Black's move, the mate would come more quickly. Make it Black's move. Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: A king does not lose a move by going back and forth. It needs a path of three squares around c2, without letting the black king out of the corner.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kc3! Kb1 2.Kd2! Ka1 3.Kc1! Ka2 4.Kc2! The position is the same as at the start, now with Black to move. The white king went around c2 via c3, d2 and c1, in four moves; the black king, caught between a1, a2 and b1, went around in three. That difference is what passes the move. 3.Kd3 on the third move also works: d2, d3 and c2 are three neighbouring squares, a real triangle. 1.Nb2 or 1.Nb6 do not spoil the win, but the knight just comes back to c4 and the job is still to be done. From there the white king goes to b3, the c4 knight closes the net and the g2 knight lets the pawn go only when the mate comes before promotion. Chéron showed that, with the black king already caught, not even a pawn well past the line saves Black.
part.triangle.title: Triangulation
part.triangle.summary: A king can pass the move by walking round three squares; a knight cannot.
part.corner.title: The right corner
part.corner.summary: With the pawn past the line and the king free, Black draws away from the mating corner. Topalov–Karpov, 2000.
step.helpWhy: 1.Ne4! The d2 knight lets go of the pawn and heads for f6. It can let go, because the pawn is no danger: it is a help. Without it, two knights cannot force mate: when the black king runs out of squares and there is no check, it is stalemate. With the pawn, Black has something to move exactly when the king cannot.
step.twoPawns: And with two pawns? One is enough to avoid stalemate, so the other can leave the board. Here the d2 pawn promotes next move. Think about which of the two White wants to keep alive. Just one rule: never capture the last pawn, because without it it is a draw.
step.captureMove.hint: 1.Nxd2: the d3 pawn stays and plays the part of the helpful pawn.
step.captureMove.done: 1.Nxd2! It was the only winning move. After 1...Kh7 it is the position from the start of the chapter, and you have seen the rest: 2.Ne4, 3.Nf6+, 4.Ne7 and 5.Ng6, mate.
step.kingBlock: And 1.Kg5? It also stops the pawn, but it is a draw. The king cannot stay put on g5: it has to help with the mate, and the moment it leaves, the pawn moves on and crosses the line. The blockader is a knight; the king stays free to push the black king.
step.d_seitz: Now a real game, with the colours reversed: Znosko-Borovsky against Seitz, Nice, 1931, the first time a master won this ending. Seitz, with Black, had the two knights. With 62...Nxf5 he captured the white bishop, and the knight stayed on f5, in front of the white pawn on f4: with the colours reversed, f4 is a square of the line. With the pawn held, Seitz spent thirty moves taking the white king to the h1 corner. Now it is time to let go.
step.d_seitz.m1: 93...Nh4. The blockading knight leaves. The pawn is free, but it needs four moves to reach f8.
step.d_seitz.m2: 94.f5. The pawn runs. Now 94...Nhxf5? would draw, and so would 94...Nexf5? Without the last pawn, two knights cannot mate.
step.d_seitz.m3: 94...Nf3+. Check, and the white king only has h1.
step.d_seitz.m4: 95.Kh1, the only move. The white king is in the corner, and the pawn on f5 still needs three moves to promote.
step.d_seitz.m5: 95...Nd1. The quiet move that decides: the knight heads for f2. The white king has no square, because g1 belongs to the f3 knight, and g2 and h2 to the black king. White has to move the pawn.
step.d_seitz.m6: 96.f6, the only move. The pawn is still two steps from f8.
step.d_seitz.m7: 96...Nf2, mate. The pawn moved only to avoid stalemate, as you saw at the start of the lesson.
step.t_tri: In Troitsky's position White could not pass the move. Here White can, and it is the king that does it. The b6 knight holds the pawn on b7, and the black king can only shuttle between b8 and a7. If it were Black's move, the mate would come quickly. How do you hand the move over?
step.t_tri.hint1: Going back and forth between two squares, the king spends two moves and it is still your move. Three squares are different.
step.t_tri.hint2: Look for three neighbouring squares, one of them b5. When the black king is on a7, the b6 knight must be defended.
step.triWhy: This is called triangulation. The white king walks round a triangle, b5, a4 and a5, and returns to b5 in three moves. The black king only has two squares, b8 and a7, and shuttles between them: after the three moves the position is the same, but with Black to move. A knight cannot do this, because it never returns to the same square in an odd number of moves. A king can. The triangles b5, b4 and a5, or b5, c4 and c5, work too.
step.d_tri: Watch the triangle move by move.
step.d_tri.m1: 1.Ka4! The king leaves b5 and starts the triangle. The b6 knight is undefended, but the black king, on b8, cannot reach it.
step.d_tri.m2: 1...Ka7, the only move: a8 and c8 belong to the b6 knight, and c7 to the e8 knight.
step.d_tri.m3: 2.Ka5! The king defends the b6 knight again, which the black king was attacking. After 2.Kb4? Black would capture the knight with 2...Kxb6.
step.d_tri.m4: 2...Kb8, the only move: a6 belongs to the white king, and the b6 knight is defended.
step.d_tri.m5: 3.Kb5. The starting position, but now Black is to move: zugzwang.
step.d_tri.m6: 3...Ka7, the only move. Now White has the move it wanted.
step.d_tri.m7: 4.Nd7! Only now does the b6 knight let the pawn go: the black king is stuck in the corner, and the mate comes before the promotion.
step.triMove: Now you, on the other side of the board. Hand the move to Black with the triangle along the edge, as in the example.
step.triMove.hint: The triangle is now g5, h4 and h5: 1.Kh4, 2.Kh5 and 3.Kg5.
step.triMove.done: The position is back, with Black to move. When the black king is caught and all you need is the move, remember the king's triangle.
step.t_corner: Now from Black's side. The pawn on h3 has already crossed the line, held by the h2 knight. The white king came to e6 to block your king's path. How do you hold the draw?
step.t_corner.hint1: The mate only works in a corner the h2 knight can reach in time after letting the pawn go. On the other side of the board it does not get there.
step.t_corner.hint2: Make the white king go back: threaten the h2 knight.
step.cornerWhy: 1...Kg5! With the pawn past the line, the mate only works in some corners. Not in the a8 corner, for instance: the h2 knight is too far away, and the moment it leaves, the pawn moves. The marked squares are the drawing zone: if the black king gets in and stays, it is a draw. The white king on e6 blocks the way in, but 1...Kg5 threatens 2...Kf4, entering the zone and heading for g3, behind the h2 knight (g4 is out: the knight covers it). White comes back with 2.Ke5, covering f4, and 2...Kg6 goes back too: if 3.Ke6, 3...Kg5 again, and White makes no progress.
step.d_karpov: Watch what happens when the king goes to the wrong corner. Monte Carlo, 2000, the Amber rapid tournament: Topalov had the two knights, and Karpov a pawn on g4, past the line, held by the g3 knight. It was a draw, but Karpov took his king to the a1 corner, where the mate works. Topalov erred with 67.Ndf5?, which gave the draw back, but Karpov erred again with 67...Kb2? From then on the net closes.
step.d_karpov.m1: 71.Nb2. The knight takes d1 and d3, and the black king only has b1.
step.d_karpov.m2: 71...Kb1, the only move. The black king is already one step from the a1 corner.
step.d_karpov.m3: 72.Nd3. The knight takes c1 and b2: the black king only has a1 and a2.
step.d_karpov.m4: 72...Ka1. The black king goes into the corner.
step.d_karpov.m5: 73.Kb3. The white king takes a2 and b2, and the black king only has b1.
step.d_karpov.m6: 73...Kb1, the only move: a2 and b2 belong to the white king. The black king can only shuttle between a1 and b1.
step.d_karpov.m7: 74.Ne2! Now the g3 knight lets the pawn go. Count: the pawn needs three moves to reach g1, and the knight gets to c3 on the next one. That is why the a1 corner lost, even far from g3. After 74...Ka1 or 74...g3 Black loses, and Karpov resigned.
step.cornerMove: Stay out of the mating corner.
step.cornerMove.hint: 1...Kg5 threatens 2...Kf4, heading for the h2 knight. If the white king goes back to e5, go back to g6.
step.cornerMove.done: 1...Kg5! and 2...Kg6. White cannot push your king out of the zone, and it is a draw.
key.seitz: Seitz, with Black, against Znosko-Borovsky, Nice, 1931: the first master win in this ending. The knight holding the pawn leaves at the right moment, and the mate comes before the promotion.
key.averbakh: The drawing zone: with the pawn past the line, Black draws if the king gets into the squares far from the blockading knight and stays there.
